prize_parts.citation: For the development of ligand-controlled palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, making the synthesis of aryl amines general and routine.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B021 alone, Buchwald and Hartwig. The chair asked for the new principle in C-N coupling, so I will state it. In C-C coupling the nucleophile arrives pre-formed as an organometallic partner and the difficult steps are not the ones that limit C-N coupling. Here a neutral amine must bind to Pd(II), be deprotonated to a palladium amido, and then undergo C-N reductive elimination, which is intrinsically slow, while the amido competes with beta-hydride elimination. The advance was to solve that kinetic problem by ligand design: chelating bisphosphines first, then bulky biaryl and hindered alkyl phosphines and well-defined precatalysts. Those ligands accelerate reductive elimination and stabilise monoligated Pd(0), and the same logic transferred across primary and secondary amines, amides, heteroaryl halides and ammonia surrogates. That is a mechanistic design principle that gave a new, general bond-forming method, with thirty years of independent confirmation and routine use in medicinal and process chemistry. Buchwald and Hartwig developed the catalytic method and its mechanism independently, so two names is a clean attribution.
statement.case_against: The 2010 prize honoured Pd cross-coupling, and Chabes, Aqvist and Linke each weigh that as a reduction in novelty or urgency. I think they are wrong on the chemistry but I accept the point is one of judgement, not proof. B021 also has the narrowest first-round support among the leaders (Borda points well below B058 and B052), and Chabes argues that sequencing opened a new measurement capability across biology while C-N coupling serves chemists. Kosugi's 1983 tin-amide reaction still leaves a priority footnote that the citation cannot fully remove, and I have not verified the chronology beyond recollection. Finally, my single-part prize is the least biology-facing option on the table and may not draw votes from members who want a broader impact case.

responses.point: Aqvist asks whether ligand design in C-N coupling is a new principle or a very successful application of the existing Pd cross-coupling framework, and says that decides whether B021 displaces base editing for him.
responses.response: I see it as a new principle. The 2010 framework (oxidative addition, transmetalation, reductive elimination) does not predict that an amine nucleophile will couple at all. Two things had to be discovered: the amido intermediate and its beta-hydride pathway, and a ligand class that makes C-N reductive elimination fast. Neither was a routine extension. The test I would apply is whether the ligand design predicted or merely rescued the reaction. It predicted it, because the ligand scaffolds were developed from the mechanism and then generalised to new substrate classes. I accept that your base editing case rests on a very clean chemical idea (hydrolytic deamination delivered by a tethered deaminase) and I rate B052 as my first alternative. My reservation remains maturity: roughly ten years against thirty, and the 2020 prize close in time. If B052 were put forward as Liu alone, I would regard the attribution as defensible but would not rank it above B021.

responses.point: Linke says he would move B021 into his top tier if the ligand-design step is shown to be the discovery, and also asks whether Kosugi's 1983 work is a priority issue or a precursor.
responses.response: The ligand-design step is the discovery, as argued in my case. On Kosugi, as I recall it his Pd-catalysed reaction of aryl bromides with tin amides was stoichiometric in tin, required toxic reagents and had narrow scope, and it did not establish a general catalytic amination. The catalytic route that avoids tin amides, using free amines with a base, came from Buchwald and Hartwig around 1994 to 1995, with the ligand generations after that. I would keep Kosugi out of the laureate list and let the citation say 'general' and 'ligand-controlled'. On generative potential versus perovskites, my doubt is that B003 is closer to materials physics and has a six-way credit problem and unresolved stability, whereas B021 has no credit or maturity problem. I take your point that a three-name cut for perovskites is genuinely contested, and that makes it a worse prize candidate for the same reason.

responses.point: Chabes agrees on attribution but sees B021 as an incremental extension of a recognised field and keeps sequencing by synthesis (Balasubramanian and Klenerman) as his first choice.
responses.response: I do not think breadth of impact separates the two. Aryl amines are in a large fraction of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals, so C-N coupling reaches well beyond chemists. On B028 I accept that the reversible-terminator chemistry is real, and the chair's question is fair. My doubt is that a two-name cut still leaves Rothberg, Mayer and Ju outside, and you have yourself said that the cut muddies a case built on Solexa chemistry. If the committee wants a biology-facing prize, I would prefer an achievement with one chemical principle and one clear driver. I have not changed my ranking because of this exchange, but I accept that B028 with its two-name core is the main competitor for my vote on chemistry-versus-technology grounds, and I rank it below B021.

responses.point: Aili places sequencing by synthesis first on the strength of the reversible-terminator and surface chemistry, but says the margin has narrowed and that he would accept a third name if the committee judged the whole field needed it.
responses.response: I appreciate that the margin has narrowed. A three-name version with Rothberg would bring in pyrosequencing, a different chemistry from the reversible terminator, and so would make the citation harder to write precisely. That is the same attribution trouble that I see in B058. I would sooner see the committee choose a part where the citation can be written in one sentence and every name on it is uncontested. I also note that you and I share B052 and B058 as alternatives, so if B021 does not reach five, these are the places where our preferences could overlap.

uncertainties: Whether members who weigh the 2010 prize heavily (Chabes, Aqvist, Linke) will accept the argument that the C-N amido and reductive-elimination problem needed its own ligand design; this is a judgement and not something I can prove.
Kosugi's chronology and the exact scope of his tin-amide reaction are from memory and unverified; this affects only whether the citation language acknowledges him.
Whether a one-part prize on a purely synthetic-methodology achievement can reach five votes when first preferences are split across at least six positions.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal to disclose. I have no known ties to Buchwald, Hartwig or Kosugi, and none of the eight members' disclosed ties changes this. My general proximity to synthetic methodology as the only synthetic organic chemist on the committee is a disclosure of bias in favour of B021, not a ground for recusal.
